text: All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter. All men tremble at punishment, all men love life; remember that thou art like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter.
context_note: The Dhammapada's argument for the first precept is analogical: from one's own fear of death to every being's. It grounds non-harm in shared sentience rather than command.

text: For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule.
context_note: Among the most cited Buddhist verses: retaliation perpetuates what it answers; only its opposite ends it. The 'old rule' claims this as timeless observation, not new doctrine.

text: Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!
context_note: Each vice is met by its counter-virtue: the practical method behind the teaching that hatred cannot end hatred.

text: If one man conquer in battle a thousand times thousand men, and if another conquer himself, he is the greatest of conquerors.
context_note: Courage is redirected inward: the battlefield hero is outranked by the one who masters his own mind — the Buddhist transvaluation of valor.

text: Not the perversities of others, not their sins of commission or omission, but his own misdeeds and negligences should a sage take notice of.
context_note: Attention to others' faults is treated as a leak in one's own practice; the verse redirects the judging eye to its owner.

text: Let him not despise what he has received, nor ever envy others: a mendicant who envies others does not obtain peace of mind.
context_note: Addressed to monks about alms, the verse generalizes: envy of another's portion destroys the calm that practice builds.

text: Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness.
context_note: Contentment is named the best wealth — the positive state whose absence envy is; the verse reorders goods by their contribution to peace.

text: He who destroys life, who speaks untruth, who in this world takes what is not given him, who goes to another man's wife; and the man who gives himself to drinking intoxicating liquors, he, even in this world, digs up his own root.
context_note: The five precepts in verse: killing, lying, taking the not-given, sexual misconduct, and intoxicants are named together as self-destruction — digging up one's own root.

text: The uncharitable do not go to the world of the gods; fools only do not praise liberality; a wise man rejoices in liberality, and through it becomes blessed in the other world.
context_note: Dana — giving — is the first of the perfections and the layperson's foundational practice; the verse ties liberality to wisdom and its refusal to folly.

text: As a mother at the risk of her life watches over her own child, her only child, so also let every one cultivate a boundless (friendly) mind towards all beings.
context_note: From the Metta Sutta: boundless friendliness toward all beings — not humans only — is the cultivated stance from which Buddhist animal ethics flows.

text: Waiting on mother and father, protecting child and wife, and a quiet calling, this is the highest blessing.
context_note: From the Mangala Sutta's list of highest blessings: service to parents stands beside care of one's own household as elemental good fortune rightly used.

text: Self is the lord of self, who else could be the lord? With self well subdued, a man finds a lord such as few can find.
context_note: Self-mastery, not self-destruction, is the path's use of this precious life; the verse is cited in Buddhist discussion of despair and of the rare opportunity a human birth affords.

text: A man is not just if he carries a matter by violence; no, he who distinguishes both right and wrong, who is learned and leads others, not by violence, but by law and equity, and who is guarded by the law and intelligent, he is called just.
context_note: Justice is defined against violence: the just judge proceeds by law and equity, not force — the verse Buddhists cite about punishment and the state's dealings with wrongdoers.

text: Do not speak harshly to anybody; those who are spoken to will answer thee in the same way. Angry speech is painful, blows for blows will touch thee.
context_note: Right speech in the eightfold path excludes the harsh and divisive; the verse's argument is again reciprocal — speech returns upon the speaker.
